coffees.name: Ethiopia Yirgacheffe Banko Chelchele Supernatural
coffees.station: Banko Chelchele station · EDN Ethiopian Coffee
coffees.processNote: Whole cherries are sorted for ripeness, sealed in a tank for about a day with no oxygen, then sun-dried on raised beds for two to four weeks with the fruit still on. EDN calls it Supernatural. That pre-drying ferment is where the blueberry and the white-wine lift come from, and the cup stays clean rather than boozy.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Coffee was born in these highlands, and this is about as close to the source as it gets. Gedeb sits in the far southeastern corner of the Gedeo Zone, officially Yirgacheffe but closer to Guji than the rest of it, and its coffees are some of the most explosive cups anywhere in Ethiopia: heady, perfume-like aromatics over a candy-sweet structure. A few hundred smallholders, each farming a hectare or two of diversified, largely organic land between 1,900 and 2,000 meters, bring ripe cherry to the Banko Chelchele station, run by EDN Ethiopian Coffee. During harvest the station employs over 200 people just to keep the drying cherry turning.

There is no single varietal to name here, and that is the point. This lot is built from heirloom landraces, the regionally adapted varieties that have grown in Ethiopia's highlands for generations, prized for their aromatic complexity and delicate florals. They are the source of the perfume that defines great Yirgacheffe. And in Ethiopia coffee is never just a drink: it is a ceremony. Beans roasted over coals in front of the guests, ground fresh, brewed in a clay jebena, and poured in rounds while the incense burns. This cup has been an occasion for a thousand years.

journey.label: Banko Chelchele · Gedeb, Ethiopia
journey.story: Arabica coffee was born in these highlands and still grows half wild under the shade trees. Gedeb hangs on the southern rim of the Gedeo Zone at nearly 2,000 meters, where a few hundred smallholder families carry cherry down the ridges to the Banko Chelchele station. West of here the land falls away toward the floor of the Great Rift Valley.

lookArounds.label: Stand in Meskel Square, Addis Ababa
lookArounds.note: Meskel Square in Addis Ababa, the capital this coffee trucks down to for milling and export, and the highest capital city in Africa. One local-shot 360; street cameras have barely reached Ethiopia.

lookArounds.label: Visit Lalibela's rock churches
lookArounds.note: Lalibela, in the northern highlands, where eleven churches were carved straight down into the living rock 800 years ago and are still in use today. A local-shot 360 from the site.

coffees.name: El Salvador Cerro Las Ranas Honey
coffees.processNote: Ripe cherries are pulped, then the beans dry on clay patios still coated in their sticky fruit mucilage, turned constantly so they dry evenly. Honey process, no bees involved. It keeps some of a natural's sweetness and red fruit while staying more consistent cup to cup.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Cerro Las Ranas means the Hill of Frogs, and the name is literal: the farm wraps around a lagoon populated by thousands of them. It sits above Apaneca in the department of Ahuachapán, along the volcanic ridge Salvadorans know as the Ruta de las Flores, with parcels climbing from 1,450 to 1,780 meters, about as high as coffee grows anywhere in the country. That altitude is what gives a honey-processed coffee this much sweetness while keeping the cup crisp.

The farm is run by JASAL, a family operation where Jose Antonio Salaverria and his sons handle everything themselves, from year-round farm management to quality control in their own cupping lab. They were honey processing this coffee years before it became one of specialty coffee's hottest trends, back when drying pulped beans in their own fruit sugar was considered a strange thing to do on purpose. The frogs, presumably, approved all along.

journey.label: Cerro Las Ranas · Apaneca, El Salvador
journey.story: The Hill of Frogs sits in the Apaneca Ilamatepec range of western El Salvador, volcano country strung with crater lakes and coffee towns. The farm is named for its lagoon and the thousands of frogs that live in it. East along this ridge the land rises to the Santa Ana volcano, the highest in the country.

lookArounds.label: Walk the streets of Apaneca
lookArounds.note: Apaneca, the little cobblestone town the farm looks down on, and one of the highest towns in El Salvador. This is the heart of the Ruta de las Flores. Drag to look around.

lookArounds.label: Stand at Laguna Verde
lookArounds.note: Down on the floor of Laguna Verde, a reed-filled crater lagoon in the cloud forest above Apaneca, cousin to the frog lagoon that gives the farm its name. One local-shot 360 from inside the crater.

coffees.name: Veracruz Finca La Laja
coffees.station: Finca La Laja · Tlaltetela, Huatusco highlands
coffees.processNote: Shade-grown under the cloud forest canopy on a farm the Sampieri family has worked since 1920.
coffees.aboutFarm: Finca La Laja sits in the La Laja community in Tlaltetela, up in the central mountains of Veracruz, somewhere between 1,130 and 1,250 meters. The whole area is fed by small tributary rivers running down into the Rio La Antigua, and the vegetation shifts as you climb: cloud forest of pine and oak higher up, giving way to tropical deciduous forest lower down. You can taste some of that range in the cup. It opens with a gentle citrus brightness and a little sweetness up front, then settles into a full, creamy body with a buttery finish that lingers without ever turning heavy. Brown sugar, toffee, cashew butter, a little lemon meringue, and underneath all of it a floral note that never quite steps forward enough to name.

journey.label: Finca La Laja · Veracruz, Mexico
journey.story: La Laja sits in the cloud forests of central Veracruz, in the mountains above Huatusco, watered by small rivers that feed the Río La Antigua. The Sampieri family has grown coffee on these slopes since 1920. On a clear day, Pico de Orizaba stands on the horizon.

lookArounds.label: Walk downtown Veracruz
lookArounds.note: Downtown Veracruz, a block off the zócalo — Mexico's oldest port city, where coffee from these mountains has shipped out for two centuries. Drag to look around; the arrows walk the streets.

lookArounds.label: Walk around El Tajín
lookArounds.note: El Tajín, a UNESCO World Heritage city of the ancient Totonac, stands a couple of hours north of the farm — the Pyramid of the Niches has 365 of them, one for each day. Drag to look around; the arrows walk the site.

coldBrew.name: One Batch Cold Brew
coldBrew.aboutFarm:
Origin TBD, but it'll be something worth the wait. Steeped 18 to 24 hours, half a gallon of water to 220 grams of grounds, a ratio strong enough that you're meant to dilute it rather than wonder where the flavor went. What comes out the other end is thick and dark, closer to a concentrate than a coffee, even though nobody around here calls it that.

Cut it with cream and a splash of water if you want it easy. A touch of sweetener if that's your thing, no judgment. Or pour it straight over ice, no water, no cream, and let it hit the way it's supposed to. That's how I drink the first glass of every batch, standing at the counter, deciding if this one's a keeper.

Brewed once, one batch, by the half gallon. When it's gone, it's gone until the next one.
